claim: SLC2A1 (GLUT1) followed by SLC2A3 (GLUT3) were the most expressed glucose transporter family members in TCGA-LUAD samples.
source: SLC2A1 (GLUT1) followed by SLC2A3 (GLUT3) were the most expressed members, (Figure 1a)
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from TCGA-LUAD shown in Figure 1a

claim: High SLC2A1 expression was correlated with poor overall survival in TCGA-LUAD.
source: high SLC2A1 expression was correlated with poor overall survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: GLUT1 protein showed intermediate and strong expression in 44% and 56% of LUAD lesions, respectively, in a human tissue microarray.
source: Specifically, it showed intermediate and strong GLUT1 expression in 44% (8/18) and 56% (10/18) of the LUAD lesions, respectively (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data from human tissue microarray shown in Figure 1b

claim: GLUT1 exhibited strong staining in all LUSC samples in the tissue microarray.
source: In LUSCs, GLUT1 exhibited strong staining in all samples (Figure 1b), confirming previous results obtained from squamous cell carcinomas of lung and other tissues (Goodwin et al., 2017; Hsieh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1b and confirmed by cited previous studies

claim: SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 were most expressed in NMF4 subtype of TCGA-LUAD.
source: SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 were the most expressed in NMF4, which contains the highest percentage of the TP53 mutation (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by NMF analysis data shown in Figure 1c

claim: NMF4 contains the highest percentage of TP53 mutation among TCGA-LUAD subtypes.
source: SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 were the most expressed in NMF4, which contains the highest percentage of the TP53 mutation (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by NMF analysis data shown in Figure 1c

claim: KP mouse model tumors are predominantly NMF4-like lesions.
source: RNA sequencing analyses of bulk tumor samples revealed a predominance of NMF4-like lesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and NMF subtype prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: Glut1 protein levels in tumor cells gradually increased along tumor progression in the KP model.
source: Glut1 protein levels in tumor cells gradually increased along tumor progression, with the majority of advanced grade lesions being positive with intermediate or strong Glut1 staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: Glut1 was only weakly expressed or undetectable in the alveolar compartment of normal lung.
source: In normal lung, Glut1 was only weakly expressed or undetectable in the alveolar compartment that comprises alveolar type-1 and 2 (AT1, AT2) cells, endothelial cells and alveolar macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b

claim: AT2 cells are considered as the principal tumor cell-of-origin in the KP model.
source: AT2 cells being considered as the principal tumor cell-of-origin in this model (Desai et al., 2014; Sutherland et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Glut1 was strongly expressed in the bronchiolar epithelial compartment containing Club cells.
source: In contrast, Glut1 was strongly expressed in the bronchiolar epithelial compartment that contains Club cells, another cell type permissive to tumor initiation (Sutherland et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and citation

claim: Club cells are another cell type permissive to tumor initiation in the KP model.
source: In contrast, Glut1 was strongly expressed in the bronchiolar epithelial compartment that contains Club cells, another cell type permissive to tumor initiation (Sutherland et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Glut1 deletion in KP tumors did not significantly reduce tumor growth rates monitored by μCT.
source: During tumor progression, we detected slightly but not significantly reduced changes in tumor growth rates monitored by X-rays micro-computed tomography (μCT) (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by μCT tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 1d

claim: No significant difference was observed in the weight of KP versus KPG1 tumors at sacrifice.
source: At sacrifice, although no significant difference was observed in the weight or in the number of lesions (Figure 1e–f)
evidence: Supported by tumor weight measurements shown in Figure 1e

claim: No significant difference was observed in the number of KP versus KPG1 lesions at sacrifice.
source: At sacrifice, although no significant difference was observed in the weight or in the number of lesions (Figure 1e–f)
evidence: Supported by tumor number counts shown in Figure 1f

claim: A significant reduction of high grade tumors (grades 4 and 5) was determined upon Glut1 loss in KP lesions.
source: a significant reduction of high grade tumors (grades 4 and 5) was determined upon Glut1 loss in KP lesions (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by tumor grading data shown in Figure 1g

claim: There was no significant increase in KPG1 mouse survival compared to KP mice.
source: Because there was no significant increase in KPG1 mouse survival (Figure 1h), these data together fail to reveal a clear impact of Glut1 deletion in the tumor epithelial cells on disease progression.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1h

claim: Glut1 deletion in tumor epithelial cells does not clearly impact disease progression in the KP model.
source: Because there was no significant increase in KPG1 mouse survival (Figure 1h), these data together fail to reveal a clear impact of Glut1 deletion in the tumor epithelial cells on disease progression.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including survival, tumor growth, and tumor grade data

claim: Intense 13C enrichments inside tumors revealed a compartmentalized intracellular accumulation of glucose-derived biomass in specific organelles.
source: Intense 13C enrichments inside tumors revealed a compartmentalized intracellular accumulation of glucose-derived biomass, which can be attributed to a specific organelle of tumor cells visualized by the superposition of images obtained from scanning EM (SEM) and NanoSIMS (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS and SEM imaging data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The organelles accumulating glucose-derived biomass resemble lamellar bodies based on their size, secretory behavior and morphology.
source: From SEM and transmission EM (TEM), these organelles resemble lamellar bodies (LBs) based on their size, secretory behavior and morphology, which exhibit more or less packed, occasionally visible lamellae (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: Supported by SEM and TEM imaging data shown in Figures 2b-c

claim: Lamellar bodies are lipid-rich secretory organelles specifically produced in the lung by AT2 cells.
source: LBs are lipid-rich secretory organelles specifically produced in the lung by AT2 cells, responsible for surfactant production and release into the alveolar space.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about lamellar bodies

claim: Lamellar bodies are responsible for surfactant production and release into the alveolar space.
source: LBs are lipid-rich secretory organelles specifically produced in the lung by AT2 cells, responsible for surfactant production and release into the alveolar space.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about lamellar body function

claim: Lamellar body-like organelles in tumor cells were typically from 200 nm to 2 μm in diameter.
source: Within tumor cells, these LB-like organelles (LBOs) were typically from 200 nm to 2 μm in diameter, irregularly shaped and darkly stained.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy observations

claim: Lamellar body-like organelles in tumor cells were irregularly shaped and darkly stained.
source: Within tumor cells, these LB-like organelles (LBOs) were typically from 200 nm to 2 μm in diameter, irregularly shaped and darkly stained.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy observations

claim: Lamellar body-like organelles often contained more heavily stained regions and discernible tightly packed lamellae at higher magnifications.
source: Often these contained more heavily stained regions and discernible tightly packed lamellae at higher magnifications (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by high-resolution TEM imaging shown in Figure 2c

claim: KPG1 tumor cells showed lower 13C-enrichment signal intensity in lamellar body-like organelles compared to KP tumor cells.
source: Quantitative NanoSIMS images of these organelles revealed a lower 13C-enrichment signal intensity in KPG1 compared to KP tumor cells (Figure 2d)
evidence: Supported by quantitative NanoSIMS measurements shown in Figure 2d

claim: The lower 13C-enrichment in KPG1 tumor cells demonstrates the consequence of Glut1 loss in vivo.
source: Quantitative NanoSIMS images of these organelles revealed a lower 13C-enrichment signal intensity in KPG1 compared to KP tumor cells (Figure 2d), demonstrating the consequence of Glut1 loss in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of 13C-enrichment between KP and KPG1 tumors

claim: KPG1 tumors failed to stimulate glycolysis in response to glucose in ex vivo experimental setting.
source: In this ex vivo experimental setting, KPG1 tumors failed to stimulate glycolysis in response to glucose (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular acidification rate measurements shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: One KPG1 tumor displayed the strongest glycolytic response of all tested tumors, which coincided with elevated expression of Glut3.
source: As exception, one KPG1 tumor displayed the strongest glycolytic response of all tested tumors, which coincided with elevated expression of another high-affinity glucose transporter, Glut3 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse measurements and Glut3 expression analysis shown in Figure 3a

claim: 'Hallmark_bile acid metabolism' was the unique significantly shared upregulated pathway between the three KPG1 cohorts compared to KP.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted, from all the Hallmark and KEGG up- and downregulated pathways, a unique significantly shared pathway between the three cohorts, which was upregulated in KPG1: 'Hallmark_bile acid metabolism' (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a

claim: Several target genes of PPARα were identified in the 'Hallmark_bile acid metabolism' pathway upregulated in KPG1.
source: Upon closer examination of the genes included in this pathway, we identified several target genes of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) (Figure 3b)
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: PPARα is a crucial transcription factor in fatty acid catabolism.
source: we identified several target genes of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) (Figure 3b), a crucial transcription factor in fatty acid catabolism (Reddy and Hashimoto, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: GSEA highlighted enrichment of known PPARα targets in KPG1 compared to KP tumors.
source: Furthermore, when interrogating the expression of known PPARα targets (Rakhshandehroo et al., 2010), GSEA highlighted their enrichment in KPG1 compared to KP tumors (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3c and citation to PPARα target genes

claim: KPG1 tumors have a stronger expression of known PPARα-target genes than KP lesions.
source: Thus, KPG1 tumors have a stronger expression of known PPARα-target genes than KP lesions.
evidence: Inferred from GSEA analysis of PPARα target genes

claim: Two possible routes for Glut1-deficient tumor growth are uptake through Glut3 or via a PPARα-dependent metabolic shift.
source: Together, our metabolic and molecular analyses suggested two possible and distinct routes for Glut1-deficient tumor growth: the uptake of the same nutrient through another glucose transporter, Glut3, or via a PPARα-dependent metabolic shift (Figure 3d).
evidence: Inferred from metabolic and molecular analyses including Seahorse data and gene expression analyses

claim: Doxycycline-mediated PPARαΔ13 induction in KP mice led only to a trend toward a reduction in tumor growth rates.
source: Doxycycline-mediated PPARαΔ13 induction in KP mice led only to a trend toward a reduction in tumor growth rates, comparable to the growth of KPG1 versus KP tumors.
evidence: Supported by μCT tumor volume measurements

claim: Within the KPG1 group, PPARαΔ13 induction did not further reduce tumor growth.
source: Within the KPG1 group, PPARαΔ13 induction did not further reduce tumor growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: Supported by μCT tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c

claim: PPARαΔ13 downregulates PPARα-related pathways in tumors.
source: Global gene expression analyses from tumor samples confirmed the functionality of the PPARαΔ13 construct in both KP and KPG1 tumors, as 'Hallmark_bile acid metabolism', 'Hallmark_fatty acid metabolism', 'KEGG_peroxisome' and 'KEGG_ fatty acid metabolism' pathways were repressed in tumors harboring this construct compared to tumors from KP-rtTA or KPG1-rtTA mice not fed on a doxycycline diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d

claim: PPARαΔ13 fails to affect tumor growth even in absence of Glut1.
source: Thus, although PPARαΔ13 downregulates PPARα-related pathways in tumors, it fails to affect their growth even in absence of Glut1.
evidence: Inferred from tumor growth measurements and gene expression analyses

claim: Slc2a3 was almost undetectable in tumors from KL mice.
source: In contrast, Slc2a3 was almost undetectable in tumors from KrasLSL-G12D; Stk11Flox/Flox (KL) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: KL mice are a lung cancer model where Lkb1-deficient tumors progress from an adeno- to a squamous histology.
source: In contrast, Slc2a3 was almost undetectable in tumors from KrasLSL-G12D; Stk11Flox/Flox (KL) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), another lung cancer model where Lkb1 (Stk11)-deficient tumors progressing from an adeno- to a squamous histology become exquisitely Glut1-dependent (Hsieh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Lkb1-deficient tumors become exquisitely Glut1-dependent.
source: In contrast, Slc2a3 was almost undetectable in tumors from KrasLSL-G12D; Stk11Flox/Flox (KL) mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), another lung cancer model where Lkb1 (Stk11)-deficient tumors progressing from an adeno- to a squamous histology become exquisitely Glut1-dependent (Hsieh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In absence of Glut1 (KLG1), Slc2a3 mRNA expression remained very low.
source: In absence of Glut1 (KLG1), Slc2a3 mRNA expression remained very low (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: Glut3 protein was undetectable by immunohistochemistry in KL and KLG1 tumors.
source: Accordingly, Glut3 protein was undetectable by immunohistochemistry in KL and KLG1 tumors, whereas it was expressed in KP and KPG1 lesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: Glut3 protein was expressed in KP and KPG1 lesions.
source: Accordingly, Glut3 protein was undetectable by immunohistochemistry in KL and KLG1 tumors, whereas it was expressed in KP and KPG1 lesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b

claim: Glut3 stained at the tumor cell membrane in 37% of small and 76% of big KP lesions.
source: More specifically, Glut3 stained at the tumor cell membrane in a minority (37%) of small and a majority (76%) of big KP lesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: Within Glut3-expressing KP tumors, areas positive for Glut3 frequently correlated with a stronger expression of Glut1.
source: Furthermore, within Glut3-expressing KP tumors, areas positive for Glut3 frequently correlated with a stronger expression of Glut1 (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d

claim: There is intra-tumor heterogeneity in glucose utilization in the KP mouse model.
source: Furthermore, within Glut3-expressing KP tumors, areas positive for Glut3 frequently correlated with a stronger expression of Glut1 (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting intra-tumor heterogeneity in glucose utilization in this mouse model, as demonstrated earlier in human non-small cell lung cancer (Hensley et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from Glut1 and Glut3 co-localization data and supported by citation to previous study in human NSCLC

claim: Intra-tumor heterogeneity in glucose utilization was demonstrated earlier in human non-small cell lung cancer.
source: Furthermore, within Glut3-expressing KP tumors, areas positive for Glut3 frequently correlated with a stronger expression of Glut1 (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting intra-tumor heterogeneity in glucose utilization in this mouse model, as demonstrated earlier in human non-small cell lung cancer (Hensley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: No differences were detected in overall tumor growth rates between KP and KPG3 animals.
source: When comparing tumor development in KP and KPG3 animals, we failed to detect differences in overall tumor growth rates, ex vivo glycolysis, mouse survival, or tumor grade distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by μCT tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a

claim: No differences were detected in ex vivo glycolysis between KP and KPG3 tumors.
source: When comparing tumor development in KP and KPG3 animals, we failed to detect differences in overall tumor growth rates, ex vivo glycolysis, mouse survival, or tumor grade distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b

claim: No differences were detected in mouse survival between KP and KPG3 animals.
source: When comparing tumor development in KP and KPG3 animals, we failed to detect differences in overall tumor growth rates, ex vivo glycolysis, mouse survival, or tumor grade distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c

claim: No differences were detected in tumor grade distribution between KP and KPG3 animals.
source: When comparing tumor development in KP and KPG3 animals, we failed to detect differences in overall tumor growth rates, ex vivo glycolysis, mouse survival, or tumor grade distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by tumor grading data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2d

claim: Glut3 deletion alone does not affect tumors in a detectable manner.
source: Although this indicates that Glut3 deletion alone does not affect tumors in a detectable manner, we next wanted to evaluate its importance in a Glut1-deficient context.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results comparing KP and KPG3 tumors

claim: Combined deletion of Glut1 and Glut3 from tumor epithelial cells resulted in a decreased number of tumors.
source: Deletion of the two glucose transporters, Glut1 and Glut3, from the tumor epithelial cell compartment resulted in a decreased number of tumors (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by tumor number counts shown in Figure 4b

claim: Combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a significant reduction of tumor growth rates monitored by μCT scans.
source: Furthermore, contrasting with our data obtained from each separately-targeted Gluts, combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a significant reduction of tumor growth rates monitored by μCT scans, to a reduced tumor size with an absence of big (>50 mg) lesions at sacrifice, to a decrease of high grade tumors, and to an extended mouse survival (Figure 4c–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: Supported by μCT tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 3a

claim: Combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a reduced tumor size with an absence of big (>50 mg) lesions at sacrifice.
source: Furthermore, contrasting with our data obtained from each separately-targeted Gluts, combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a significant reduction of tumor growth rates monitored by μCT scans, to a reduced tumor size with an absence of big (>50 mg) lesions at sacrifice, to a decrease of high grade tumors, and to an extended mouse survival (Figure 4c–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: Supported by tumor weight and area measurements shown in Figures 4d-e

claim: Combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a decrease of high grade tumors.
source: Furthermore, contrasting with our data obtained from each separately-targeted Gluts, combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a significant reduction of tumor growth rates monitored by μCT scans, to a reduced tumor size with an absence of big (>50 mg) lesions at sacrifice, to a decrease of high grade tumors, and to an extended mouse survival (Figure 4c–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: Supported by tumor grading data shown in Figure 4f

claim: Combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to an extended mouse survival.
source: Furthermore, contrasting with our data obtained from each separately-targeted Gluts, combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion led to a significant reduction of tumor growth rates monitored by μCT scans, to a reduced tumor size with an absence of big (>50 mg) lesions at sacrifice, to a decrease of high grade tumors, and to an extended mouse survival (Figure 4c–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4g

claim: The synergistic action of dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion was demonstrated in vitro with four different human NSCLC cell lines.
source: This synergistic action of the dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion was also demonstrated in vitro with four different human NSCLC cell lines, on which the strongest reduction of tumor cell viability resulted from the combined knockdown of these glucose transporters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c–f).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c-f

claim: The strongest reduction of tumor cell viability resulted from the combined knockdown of Glut1 and Glut3 in human NSCLC cell lines.
source: This synergistic action of the dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion was also demonstrated in vitro with four different human NSCLC cell lines, on which the strongest reduction of tumor cell viability resulted from the combined knockdown of these glucose transporters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c–f).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c-f

claim: Glut1 and Glut3 function as a coordinated glucose transport unit required to fuel the growth of LUAD.
source: Together, these data position Glut1 and Glut3 as a coordinated glucose transport unit required to fuel the growth of LUAD.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing synergistic effects of dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion

claim: Glut1-deficient KP tumors incorporated significantly less 18F-FDG than control lesions.
source: The maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of each tumor revealed that Glut1-deficient KP tumors incorporated significantly less 18F-FDG than control lesions (Figure 4h–i)
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG-PET measurements shown in Figures 4h-i

claim: Glut3-deficient and control KP tumors presented a similar 18F-FDG absorption.
source: Glut3-deficient and control KP tumors presented a similar 18F-FDG absorption (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG-PET measurements shown in Figures 4h-i

claim: In absence of Glut3, lesions might incorporate 18F-FDG via Glut1 because Glut3 positive KP tumors mainly co-express Glut1 and Glut3.
source: This result might be explained by the fact that Glut3 positive KP tumors mainly co-express Glut1 and Glut3 (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1d). Thus, in absence of Glut3, lesions might certainly incorporate 18F-FDG via Glut1.
evidence: Inferred from Glut1 and Glut3 co-expression data and 18F-FDG-PET results

claim: The 18F-FDG absorption of Glut1- and Glut3-deficient KP tumors was significantly reduced as compared to control KP lesions.
source: The 18F-FDG absorption of Glut1- and Glut3-deficient KP tumors was significantly reduced as compared to control KP lesions (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG-PET measurements shown in Figures 4h-i

claim: Most tumors analyzed had not yet gained Glut3 expression and become dependent on it, which agrees with an elevated Glut3 expression specifically in big lesions.
source: Because glucose uptake was not significantly lower in KPG3 compared to KP tumors, and in KPG1G3 compared to KPG1 tumors, a possible explanation is that most tumors analyzed had not yet gained Glut3 expression and become dependent on it, which agrees with an elevated Glut3 expression specifically in big lesions (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Inferred from 18F-FDG-PET results and Glut3 expression data in small versus big lesions

claim: The expression of no other glucose transporter was changed upon dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion in KP tumors.
source: Finally, to investigate if Glut1- and Glut3-deficient tumors might incorporate glucose via another glucose transporter, we performed a gene expression analysis of glucose transporter family members on KP and KPG1G3 lesions. This analysis showed that the expression of no other glucose transporter was changed upon dual Glut1 and Glut3 deletion in KP tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a

claim: Deleting Glut1 and Glut3 in KP tumors reduces glucose uptake.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that deleting Glut1 and Glut3 in KP tumors reduces glucose uptake, and that Glut1 highly contributes to glucose uptake in KP tumors.
evidence: Inferred from 18F-FDG-PET measurements and NanoSIMS data

claim: Glut1 highly contributes to glucose uptake in KP tumors.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that deleting Glut1 and Glut3 in KP tumors reduces glucose uptake, and that Glut1 highly contributes to glucose uptake in KP tumors.
evidence: Inferred from 18F-FDG-PET measurements showing significant reduction in KPG1 tumors

claim: At least a part of the remaining 18F-FDG-PET signal detected in KPG1G3 tumors might come from glucose uptake by the cells of the tumor immune microenvironment.
source: These results may also lead to the hypothesis that at least a part of the remaining 18F-FDG-PET signal detected in KPG1G3 tumors might come from glucose uptake by the cells of the tumor immune microenvironment.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on remaining 18F-FDG signal in KPG1G3 tumors

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Sglt2 showed its role in premalignant KP lung lesions.
source: Recently, pharmacological inhibition of a secondary active, Na+-dependent glucose transporter, Sglt2, showed its role in premalignant KP lung lesions (Scafoglio et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: A glycolytic switch was identified in advanced compared to early KP tumors.
source: while a glycolytic switch was identified in advanced compared to early tumors (Kerr et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Glucose utilization is important for LUAD development in vivo.
source: These studies, together with our gene targeting approaches, definitively demonstrate the importance of glucose utilization for LUAD development in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from current study results and cited previous studies

claim: Glut1 deletion impairs LUSC development in the KL model.
source: In the KL model, Glut1 deletion impairs LUSC development (Hsieh et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Lkb1-deficient lung tumors lack detectable Glut3, precluding any compensation occurring through this transporter.
source: and we find that Lkb1-deficient lung tumors lack detectable Glut3, precluding any compensation occurring through this transporter.
evidence: Supported by Glut3 expression data from KL and KLG1 tumors

claim: Trp53-deficient tumor cells depend on glucose uptake based on a redundant system, whereby the expression of either Glut1 or Glut3 is sufficient to sustain tumor growth.
source: In contrast, in pure LUAD our results indicate that Trp53-deficient tumor cells depend on glucose uptake based on a redundant system, whereby the expression of either Glut1 or Glut3 is sufficient to sustain tumor growth (Figure 4j).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing that only combined Glut1 and Glut3 deletion impairs tumor growth

claim: Dual Glut1 and Glut3 blockade will be necessary to achieve strong anti-tumor efficacy.
source: For clinical perspectives, we anticipate that dual Glut1 and Glut3 blockade will be necessary to achieve strong anti-tumor efficacy.
evidence: Speculative statement based on experimental results showing synergistic effects of dual deletion

claim: Glucose transporters are the first and rate-limiting step for cellular glucose utilization.
source: Glucose transporters are the first and rate-limiting step for cellular glucose utilization, a process often exacerbated in tumor cells that enables their growth and proliferation (Ancey et al., 2018; Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Glucose utilization is a process often exacerbated in tumor cells that enables their growth and proliferation.
source: Glucose transporters are the first and rate-limiting step for cellular glucose utilization, a process often exacerbated in tumor cells that enables their growth and proliferation (Ancey et al., 2018; Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Inhibiting glucose metabolism in lung tumors could become an efficient treatment strategy.
source: Although inhibiting glucose metabolism in lung tumors could become an efficient treatment strategy (Hensley et al., 2016; Patra et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: It remains unclear whether and which glucose transporter(s) should be targeted because of their possible functional redundancy.
source: whether and which glucose transporter(s) should be targeted remains unclear because of their possible functional redundancy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about glucose transporter redundancy

claim: In solid cancers, tumor cell growth can be fueled by nutrients other than glucose.
source: Additionally, in solid cancers, tumor cell growth can be fueled by nutrients other than glucose, or by using transporter-independent metabolic processes including autophagy and macropinocytosis (Commisso et al., 2013; Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2017; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Tumor cell growth can be fueled by transporter-independent metabolic processes including autophagy and macropinocytosis.
source: Additionally, in solid cancers, tumor cell growth can be fueled by nutrients other than glucose, or by using transporter-independent metabolic processes including autophagy and macropinocytosis (Commisso et al., 2013; Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2017; Son et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Lamellar body-like organelles in tumor cells are the primary site of glucose-derived biomass accumulation.
source: By glucose tracing and ultrastructural analyses, we identified the presence of lamellar body-like organelles in tumor cells, which are the primary site of glucose-derived biomass accumulation, occurring partly in a Glut1-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS and electron microscopy data

claim: Glucose-derived biomass accumulation in lamellar body-like organelles occurs partly in a Glut1-dependent manner.
source: By glucose tracing and ultrastructural analyses, we identified the presence of lamellar body-like organelles in tumor cells, which are the primary site of glucose-derived biomass accumulation, occurring partly in a Glut1-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS data showing reduced 13C-enrichment in KPG1 tumors

claim: The deletion of Glut1 or Glut3 alone in cancer cells does not impair tumor growth in the KP model.
source: In a genetically-engineered mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma, we show that the deletion of only one highly expressed glucose transporter, Glut1 or Glut3, in cancer cells does not impair tumor growth, whereas their combined loss diminishes tumor development.
evidence: Supported by tumor growth, survival, and grading data from KPG1 and KPG3 mice

claim: Combined loss of Glut1 and Glut3 diminishes tumor development in the KP model.
source: In a genetically-engineered mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma, we show that the deletion of only one highly expressed glucose transporter, Glut1 or Glut3, in cancer cells does not impair tumor growth, whereas their combined loss diminishes tumor development.
evidence: Supported by tumor growth, survival, and grading data from KPG1G3 mice

claim: 18F-FDG-PET analyses demonstrate that Glut1 and Glut3 loss decreases glucose uptake in tumors.
source: 18F-FDG-PET analyses of tumors demonstrate that Glut1 and Glut3 loss decreases glucose uptake, which is mainly dependent on Glut1.

claim: Glucose uptake in KP tumors is mainly dependent on Glut1.
